name: paperform
title: Paperform
summary: A paper and motion typography studio. Design dimensional cards, animate words, and create shareable posters with fonts, stickers, textures, and custom colors.

caseStudy.problem: Make expressive paper cards and animated typography approachable in one browser-based creative tool.
caseStudy.role: Product design, visual identity, interactive editing, animation rendering, and export workflows.
caseStudy.constraints: Run entirely in the browser without accounts, paid APIs, or a backend.
caseStudy.process: Built connected Fold and Motion workspaces with editable templates, a creative-material library, timeline controls, and shared rendering for card previews and image exports.
caseStudy.result: A standalone studio for interactive cards and animated posters, with local autosave, editable backups, share links, PNG and print exports, and browser-recorded video.
features: Ten distinct card templates, bundled fonts, stickers, textures, frames, and custom colors
Wave, spring, liquid, and particle text effects with draggable layers and timeline controls
Fold-linked animations, square and portrait posters, and landscape compositions
Shareable designs, editable backups, PNG postcards, printable cards, and video exports
engineering: CSS 3D fold previews and Canvas typography rendering
Validated design imports and Unicode-safe share links
Bundled fonts and shared card rendering for previews and exports
Browser-native video recording with preview and cancellation

name: pocket-planet
title: Pocket Planet
summary: A living 3D ecosystem in miniature. Shape terrain, introduce wildlife, change the weather, and discover how small changes ripple through your planet.

caseStudy.statement: Make a little change. Watch a whole world respond.
caseStudy.problem: Make ecosystem relationships tangible through a playful, interactive world that invites experimentation.
caseStudy.role: Game design, 3D rendering, ecosystem simulation, responsive interface, and save-file validation.
caseStudy.constraints: Run entirely in the browser with no accounts, API keys, or backend, while keeping simulation state bounded and portable.
caseStudy.process: Built eight terrain materials, elevation sculpting, twelve interacting species, seasons, optional disasters, habitat missions, and a discovery journal around a rotatable 3D planet.
caseStudy.result: A standalone ecosystem sandbox with ocean exploration, family histories, living terrain, controlled experiments, timeline branching, shareable seeds, and compatible backups.
features: Eight terrain materials with mountain, valley, and lake-depth sculpting
Twelve species, underwater gardens, animal tracking, and family histories
Eight missions, evolving landscapes, and controlled ecosystem experiments
Planet templates, shareable seeds, timeline replay, branching, and creative building
engineering: Three.js rendering with reusable geometry and materials
Deterministic ecosystem simulation and bounded populations
Validated JSON imports and browser-local autosave
Tests for habitat rules, climate effects, long runs, and save roundtrips

name: side-quest
title: Side Quest
summary: Small adventures for everyday life. Match a quest to your mood, follow its prompts, and collect memories in a personal passport.

caseStudy.statement: Turn a spare fifteen minutes into a story worth keeping.
caseStudy.problem: Help people break out of everyday routines with approachable activities that fit their time, budget, and mood.
caseStudy.role: Product design, original SVG illustration, responsive frontend, quest matching, and browser persistence.
caseStudy.constraints: Work without accounts, paid APIs, or location permissions while keeping personal notes on the device.
caseStudy.process: Created sixteen guided adventures, constraint-based discovery, completion checklists, and a collectible passport.
caseStudy.result: A standalone app with preference matching, persistent stamps and notes, shareable quest links, and downloadable memories.
features: Sixteen adventures across Explore, Create, Recharge, and Connect
Matching by time, budget, mood, and setting
Guided checklists and a collectible stamp passport
Private notes, quest links, and text export
engineering: Vite and JavaScript with original SVG artwork
Browser-local persistence without a backend
Native dialogs, keyboard controls, and responsive layouts
Tests for catalogue integrity and matching edge cases

name: petty-court
title: Petty Court
summary: A playful court of public opinion for everyday disputes. File a case, present evidence, invite a jury, and share the verdict.

caseStudy.statement: A tiny disagreement deserves an unnecessarily beautiful hearing.
caseStudy.problem: Give friends a playful, structured way to settle low-stakes disagreements while making evidence and both sides of the story easy to understand.
caseStudy.role: Product design, visual identity, responsive frontend, case and voting APIs, data persistence, and validation.
caseStudy.constraints: Keep filing and voting account-free, preserve shared case state, prevent duplicate votes within a browser, and handle deadlines and owner-only case closure.
caseStudy.process: Built a searchable docket, a three-step filing flow, evidence exhibits, jury voting, and verdict cards. Local development uses persistent files; the PostgreSQL adapter serializes hosted writes with row locks.
caseStudy.result: A standalone app with public case links, image and text evidence, timed voting, case-owner controls, and exportable verdict cards. Deployment requires a PostgreSQL connection.
features: Searchable and filterable case docket with clearly labeled fictional examples
Three-step filing with up to three image or text exhibits
Browser-based voting, jury deadlines, and owner-only early closure
Shareable case links and downloadable verdict cards
engineering: Next.js and React with TypeScript and a custom responsive visual system
Atomic local persistence and a PostgreSQL-backed deployment adapter
Server-side validation, request-size limits, origin checks, and protected ownership
Tests for verdicts, deadlines, concurrent transactions, and HTTP workflows

name: bad-ui-olympics
title: Bad UI Olympics
summary: Six absurd timed challenges: spinning PIN digits, unhelpful volume buttons, a relocating submit button, backwards checkboxes, a scrambled elevator, and a password puzzle.

caseStudy.problem: Turn familiar interface frustrations into a short, funny game visitors can immediately play.
caseStudy.role: Game design, visual direction, and frontend implementation.
caseStudy.constraints: Keep the game playable with mouse, touch, and keyboard, without accounts or external services.
caseStudy.process: Built six distinct challenges with timed rounds, paused intermissions, a browser-local personal best, and copyable results.
caseStudy.result: A six-event browser game with medal thresholds, individual event times, replay, and shareable scores.
caseStudy.statement: Sometimes the best way to appreciate good design is to race through bad design.
features: Six timed events with paused intermissions
Medals, browser-local personal best, replay, and copyable scores
engineering: React state and interval cleanup for game transitions
Monotonic timing excludes intermissions
Keyboard and touch controls with scoped responsive styles

name: tempo
title: Tempo
summary: A personal focus workspace connecting a Kanban board, Pomodoro timer, notes, goals, and habits.

caseStudy.statement: I can connect everyday planning with reliable timing, private data, and meaningful progress tracking.
caseStudy.problem: Tasks, focus sessions, notes, and habits often live in separate tools. Tempo brings them into one workspace so a plan can become focused work and a useful record of progress.
caseStudy.role: Product design, React and TypeScript frontend, FastAPI backend, data modeling, authentication, timer behavior, and automated testing.
caseStudy.constraints: Timers must survive refreshes and background tabs without losing accuracy. Private records must remain isolated between accounts, completed sessions must not be counted twice, and goals and reviews must respect calendar boundaries.
caseStudy.process: I connected task cards to a shared focus timer, then added notes, subtasks, goals, habits, and review views. Server-side ownership checks protect each account, while deadline-based timing and transactional session saves keep progress consistent.
caseStudy.result: A full-stack workspace with private boards, focus history, personal notes, habit streaks, progress reviews, customizable themes and timers, and a temporary demo that can be explored without signing up.
features: Kanban tasks with priorities, session estimates, notes, and subtasks
Pomodoro sessions and breaks with refresh recovery and optional completion alerts
Private scratchpad, automatic or manual goals, and weekday-based habit tracking
Weekly and monthly reviews of focus sessions, completed tasks, and habits
Personal themes and timer styles, account settings, and a 24-hour sample workspace
engineering: React, TypeScript, and Vite frontend paired with a FastAPI and Pydantic backend
PostgreSQL support for hosting and SQLite for local development
Salted scrypt password hashes, HttpOnly sessions, CSRF checks, and account-scoped queries
Deadline-based timing and transactional saves prevent drift and duplicate session records
Backend and frontend tests cover account isolation, timer recovery, calendar boundaries, and interface workflows

name: workio
title: Workio
summary: A connected workspace that brings freelancers, clients, projects, messages, time, and billing together.

caseStudy.statement: I can model and build a connected, permission-aware business workflow—not just isolated CRUD screens.
caseStudy.problem: Freelancers often manage leads, project scope, client communication, schedules, files, time, expenses, and invoices across disconnected tools. Workio brings that lifecycle into one workspace shared by freelancers and clients.
caseStudy.role: Product design, workflow modeling, Django architecture, backend and frontend implementation, authorization, data design, testing, and deployment preparation.
caseStudy.constraints: Freelancers and clients need different permissions over the same records. Financial data must stay traceable, invitations must expire safely, uploaded files must remain private, and state changes across proposals, milestones, time entries, expenses, and invoices must stay consistent.
caseStudy.process: I modeled the freelance lifecycle as connected Django apps for accounts, projects, conversations, billing, and notifications. I built role-scoped querysets and permission checks first, then layered in reusable work templates, intake forms, proposals, scheduling, milestones, activity history, messaging, time tracking, expenses, invoicing, and dashboard summaries.
caseStudy.result: A tested full-stack client portal where freelancers can move work from inquiry and proposal through delivery and payment while clients collaborate, review milestones, exchange files and messages, and track the same source of truth.
features: Freelancer and client accounts with public profiles, invitations, and role-aware dashboards
Projects with tasks, milestones, files, comments, activity history, saved views, and workflow stages
Proposals, service offerings, intake questions, schedules, recurring work, and payment installments
Private conversations, attachments, unread states, and in-app or email notifications
Live timers, manual time entries, expenses, invoices, and traceable invoice line items
engineering: Django 5.2 domain apps keep accounts, projects, communication, billing, and notifications separated
Server-side authorization and user-scoped querysets protect shared project and financial records
Database constraints and transactional updates prevent duplicate billing and conflicting active timers
PostgreSQL is supported in production while SQLite keeps the local demo easy to run
Django test coverage exercises permissions, workflows, billing rules, notification delivery, and dashboard calculations

name: kiki-world
title: Kiki World
summary: A story-driven 3D studio where an animated avatar explores a playful, interactive world.

caseStudy.statement: I can build polished, performant interactive 3D experiences.
caseStudy.problem: Turn isolated Three.js experiments into one coherent experience with a clear journey and purpose.
caseStudy.role: Creative direction, interaction design, 3D frontend architecture, animation, accessibility, and performance engineering.
caseStudy.constraints: The scene needs to feel rich on desktop while remaining controllable on touch devices, respectful of reduced-motion preferences, and useful when a device cannot sustain the full visual workload.
caseStudy.process: I made the rooms the narrative structure, then integrated the avatar as the visitor. Input is normalized across keyboard, pointer, and touch, while intentional camera transitions and interaction cues make each space understandable.
caseStudy.result: A responsive three-room experience in which Kiki walks between Make, Rest, and Connect, changes outfits, and transitions into room-specific activities while the camera and rendering quality adapt to the device.
features: Three explorable rooms with distinct stories, lighting, and avatar activities
Blended walking, waving, typing, sitting, dancing, and idle animation states
Four switchable outfits that preserve the active room and journey state
Wheel, keyboard, click, swipe, touch, and compact mobile navigation
Loading progress, reduced-motion behavior, and manual or automatic performance modes
engineering: Next.js and TypeScript provide the application shell around React Three Fiber and Three.js
Horizontal root motion is removed from Mixamo clips so the avatar remains aligned with room destinations
Responsive camera framing adapts to portrait, landscape, and short-screen layouts
Adaptive device-pixel ratio and performance monitoring reduce detail when sustained frame rate declines
Only the six animation clips used by the experience are shipped and GLB assets are preloaded

name: kiki-arcade
title: Kiki Arcade
summary: A colorful collection of creative toys, arcade classics, and miniature browser adventures.

caseStudy.statement: I can turn small experiments into one cohesive, polished, and maintainable interactive product.
caseStudy.problem: Several earlier projects—Ganvas, Ticking Room, Pocket Calc, and Hand Game—were too small to stand alone in a portfolio. The challenge was to preserve what made each one playful while combining them with new games into a collection that felt intentional rather than like a list of disconnected demos.
caseStudy.role: Product direction, visual design, game design, frontend architecture, implementation, accessibility, testing, and deployment.
caseStudy.constraints: Fourteen experiences with different controls and rendering needs had to coexist in one dependency-light app, work across keyboard, pointer, touch, and swipe input, preserve local progress, respect reduced-motion preferences, and clean up timers, animation frames, audio, and event listeners when players changed games.
caseStudy.process: I grouped the collection into Featured Adventures, Creative Studio, and Arcade Classics, then gave every experience a shared launcher and game-page shell. Each game is an independently mounted module with its own state and cleanup function. I rebuilt the original experiments, added five larger adventures and familiar beginner games, unified the visual system, and extracted pure game logic so it could be tested outside the interface.
caseStudy.result: A responsive arcade containing 14 complete browser experiences—from pixel drawing and ambient interaction to puzzle, strategy, platform, flight, and classic games—with persistent records, accessible controls, reduced-motion support, generated audio cues, and 22 automated logic tests.
features: Five miniature adventures: Garden Serpent, Night Shift, Parcel Quest, Patchwork Odyssey, and Paper Skies
Five creative experiences, including Ganvas with drag drawing, erasing, flood fill, undo, rainbow paint, and PNG export
Four polished arcade classics with saved wins, streaks, move records, and personal bests
Responsive keyboard, pointer, touch, swipe, and on-screen controls
Local progress, scores, unlocks, and motion preferences without requiring an account
engineering: Vite and native ES modules keep the runtime small and avoid a UI-framework dependency
Independent mount and cleanup functions prevent games from leaking listeners, timers, animation frames, or audio
Canvas powers drawing, defense, delivery, platforming, flight, and Snake-style gameplay where frame-based rendering is useful
Pure domain functions cover scoring, collisions, movement, flood filling, recipes, puzzles, routes, and flight physics with Node's test runner
Semantic controls, live status text, focus states, and prefers-reduced-motion support improve accessibility

name: booktrace
title: Booktrace
summary: A personal reading history for reviews, ratings, notes, and reading goals.

caseStudy.statement: I can design and ship a complete, reliable full-stack application around real user data.
caseStudy.problem: A basic book log could save titles and notes, but it did not yet feel like a trustworthy personal product. Readers needed private libraries, richer reading context, useful progress views, resilient discovery, and safe ownership rules for every mutation.
caseStudy.role: Product direction, UX and visual design, full-stack architecture, database modeling, authentication, validation, external API integration, accessibility, testing, and deployment.
caseStudy.constraints: Every library record must remain private to its owner, external book providers can be slow or unavailable, untrusted form data needs server-side validation, and database migrations must deploy safely without sacrificing responsive loading, empty, and error states.
caseStudy.process: I rebuilt the project around Auth.js sessions and owner-scoped Prisma queries, expanded the data model for reading status, ratings, tags, favorites, dates, goals, and profile settings, and validated server actions with Zod. Search uses Google Books first and automatically falls back to Open Library, while saved metadata snapshots keep personal entries useful during provider outages.
caseStudy.result: A production-ready private reading companion with authentication, personal libraries, five reading states, reviews and notes, yearly goals and statistics, resilient search, account controls, accessible responsive states, and automated validation and mapping tests.
features: Private accounts and libraries protected by Auth.js credential sessions
Reading states, 1–5 ratings, tags, favorites, reviews, notes, and reading dates
Annual goals, progress indicators, and library statistics
Google Books discovery with timeouts, caching, and automatic Open Library fallback
Profile settings and password-confirmed account deletion
engineering: Next.js 16 server components and server actions keep private reads and mutations on the server
Every Prisma library query is scoped by userId and the database enforces one entry per user and book
Zod validates untrusted form data before mutations and bcrypt protects stored passwords
Validated book snapshots decouple saved entries from external-provider availability
Vitest and Testing Library cover domain validation, external-data mapping, and key interface behavior
